## Four ways to represent a function

### Exercise 1.1

For $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$, give a verbal description, an algebraic rule, a table for $x=0,1,2,3,4$, and enough graph features to sketch it. State its domain and range.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
The rule squares the input, subtracts four times the input, then adds three. Completing the square gives $f(x)=(x-2)^2-1$.

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $f(x)$ | 3 | 0 | -1 | 0 | 3 |

The graph is an upward-opening parabola with vertex $(2,-1)$ and axis $x=2$. It crosses the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(3,0)$, and the $y$-axis at $(0,3)$. Its domain is $\mathbb R$; since $(x-2)^2\geq0$, its range is $[-1,\infty)$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 1.2

A parking garage charges $\$3$ for the first hour and $\$2$ for each additional **started** hour, up to four hours. Describe the cost verbally, give a formula on $0<t\leq4$, make a table for $t=0.5,1,1.2,2.7,4$, and describe its graph.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
After the first hour, each new hour begins a new $\$2$ charge. Thus
$$
C(t)=\begin{cases}3,&0<t\leq1,\\5,&1<t\leq2,\\7,&2<t\leq3,\\9,&3<t\leq4.\end{cases}
$$

The requested costs are $3,3,5,7,9$ dollars, respectively. The graph is a step function: each horizontal segment has an open circle at its left endpoint and a closed circle at its right endpoint. For example, $(1,3)$ is included, while $(1,5)$ is not. The domain is $(0,4]$ and the range is $\{3,5,7,9\}$.
:::
::::

## Mathematical models: a catalog of essential functions

### Exercise 1.3

A sample starts with $80$ mg of a substance and loses $15\%$ of its mass each hour. Write a model for its mass after $t$ hours, compute the mass after $3$ hours, and find when the mass first falls below $40$ mg.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Each hour retains $100\%-15\%=85\%$ of the previous mass, so the exponential model is $M(t)=80(0.85)^t$ mg for $t\geq0$. At $t=3$,
$$M(3)=80(0.85)^3=49.13\text{ mg (approximately).}$$
To solve $80(0.85)^t<40$, divide by $80$ and take logarithms:
$$t\ln(0.85)<\ln(0.5).$$
Because $\ln(0.85)<0$, division reverses the inequality:
$$t>\frac{\ln(0.5)}{\ln(0.85)}\approx4.27.$$
In continuous time the threshold is crossed just after $4.27$ hours; at hourly readings, the first below-half reading is at hour $5$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 1.4

A wheel has radius $2$ m and its center is $3$ m above the ground. A marked point begins at the wheel's lowest point and the wheel makes one revolution every $8$ s. Model the point's height $h(t)$ and find its height at $t=2$ s.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
The midline is $3$ m, amplitude is $2$ m, and angular frequency is $2\pi/8=\pi/4$ radians per second. A cosine starts at a maximum, so a negative cosine starts at the lowest point:
$$h(t)=3-2\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right).$$
At $t=0$, this gives $1$ m as required. At $t=2$, the angle is $\pi/2$, so $h(2)=3-2(0)=3$ m. The range is $[1,5]$ m and the period is $8$ s.
:::
::::

## The limit of a function

### Exercise 1.5

Let $f(x)=(x^2-9)/(x-3)$ for $x\ne3$, and define $f(3)=100$. Find $\lim_{x\to3}f(x)$ and explain why the assigned value at $x=3$ does not change the limit.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
For $x\ne3$, factor and cancel:
$$f(x)=\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=x+3.$$
As $x$ approaches $3$ through nearby values, $x+3$ approaches $6$. Therefore $\lim_{x\to3}f(x)=6$. A limit uses values with $x\ne3$ arbitrarily close to $3$; the isolated value $f(3)=100$ has no effect.
:::
::::

### Exercise 1.6

For $g(x)=|x|/x$ when $x\ne0$, find the left-hand and right-hand limits at $0$. Does $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)$ exist?

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
If $x<0$, then $|x|=-x$ and $g(x)=-1$, so $\lim_{x\to0^-}g(x)=-1$. If $x>0$, then $|x|=x$ and $g(x)=1$, so $\lim_{x\to0^+}g(x)=1$. A two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits agree. They do not, so the limit does not exist.
:::
::::

## Calculating limits using the limit laws

### Exercise 1.7

Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{(x^2+1)(3x-1)}{x+3}$, indicating where limit laws apply.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Polynomials are continuous, and the denominator tends to $2+3=5\ne0$, so the product and quotient limit laws permit direct substitution:
$$\lim_{x\to2}\frac{(x^2+1)(3x-1)}{x+3}
=\frac{(2^2+1)(3\cdot2-1)}{2+3}
=\frac{5\cdot5}{5}=5.$$
:::
::::

### Exercise 1.8

Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{x}$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Direct substitution gives $0/0$, so first multiply by the conjugate:
$$\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{x}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{4+x}+2}{\sqrt{4+x}+2}
=\frac{(4+x)-4}{x(\sqrt{4+x}+2)}
=\frac1{\sqrt{4+x}+2},\qquad x\ne0.$$
The denominator now tends to $4$, so the quotient law gives the limit $1/4$.
:::
::::

## The precise definition of a limit

### Exercise 1.9

Use the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition to prove that $\lim_{x\to2}(3x+1)=7$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Let $\varepsilon>0$ be given. We need $|(3x+1)-7|<\varepsilon$ whenever $0<|x-2|<\delta$. Since
$$|(3x+1)-7|=3|x-2|,$$
choose $\delta=\varepsilon/3$. Then $0<|x-2|<\delta$ implies $|(3x+1)-7|<3\delta=\varepsilon$. This proves the limit.
:::
::::

### Exercise 1.10

Use the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition to prove that $\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4$. Give an explicit $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Factor $|x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|$. To control the second factor, first require $|x-2|<1$. Then $1<x<3$ and $|x+2|<5$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose
$$\delta=\min\left\{1,\frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right\}.$$
If $0<|x-2|<\delta$, then $|x^2-4|<5|x-2|<5\delta\leq\varepsilon$. This is exactly the required definition.
:::
::::

## Continuity

### Exercise 1.11

Find $k$ so that $f(x)=\begin{cases}(x^2-1)/(x-1),&x\ne1,\\k,&x=1\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=1$.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Continuity at $1$ requires $f(1)=\lim_{x\to1}f(x)$. For $x\ne1$,
$$\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1.$$
Thus the limit is $1+1=2$. Since $f(1)=k$, the only choice is $k=2$.
:::
::::

### Exercise 1.12

Use continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that $x^3+x-1=0$ has a solution between $0$ and $1$. Explain why that solution is unique.

:::: {.content-visible unless-profile="student"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show solution"}
Let $p(x)=x^3+x-1$. As a polynomial, $p$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. It has $p(0)=-1<0$ and $p(1)=1>0$, so the Intermediate Value Theorem gives a $c\in(0,1)$ with $p(c)=0$.

For uniqueness, $p'(x)=3x^2+1>0$ for every real $x$. Therefore $p$ is strictly increasing and can cross zero at most once. Hence the solution in $(0,1)$ is unique.
:::
::::
